title: The India-US Trade Deal Is Taking Shape — but a USTR Investigation Threatens to Derail It
excerpt: A US delegation is expected in New Delhi next month, yet the shadow of Section 301 tariffs looms over what could be the most consequential bilateral pact in a decade
body:
The contours of a new India-US trade agreement are becoming visible. A high-level American delegation is expected to visit New Delhi in June for the next round of negotiations under the bilateral trade agreement framework that both countries have been quietly assembling since February. India's Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal confirmed the visit is being planned, though specific dates remain unfinished.

The stakes are substantial. Bilateral trade between the two countries reached $140 billion in FY2025-26, with Indian exports to the US rising marginally to $87.3 billion and American imports climbing a more robust 15.95 per cent to $52.9 billion. Indian firms have pledged $20.5 billion in fresh investments in the United States, with 12 companies committing $1.1 billion in a single ceremony on 6 May — a gesture designed to demonstrate that India is not merely seeking market access but is willing to create American jobs in return.

## The interim pact

The negotiating architecture is a two-step process. The first is an interim trade pact — a quick-win agreement covering areas where both sides can show progress without resolving their deeper disagreements. This is expected to include expanded market access for American agricultural products, streamlined customs procedures, and commitments on digital trade and data localisation.

The second, more ambitious step is a comprehensive bilateral trade agreement that would address tariffs, intellectual property, services trade, and investment protections. This is the deal that both governments want but neither is confident they can deliver quickly.

The interim pact is modelled on a pragmatic calculation: give both leaders something to announce before the political calendar closes their windows. Modi, fresh from his five-nation European tour, needs to demonstrate that India is not being sidelined in the global trade realignment. The Trump administration, facing midterm-season scrutiny over its tariff policies, needs to show that its trade strategy produces deals, not just disruptions.

## The Section 301 shadow

The optimism, however, runs into a hard obstacle. The Office of the United States Trade Representative is conducting an active Section 301 investigation into Indian trade practices — the same legal tool that was used to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods in 2018. The investigation covers India's digital services tax, data localisation requirements, and alleged barriers to American e-commerce and financial services firms.

For the Indian side, the investigation is more than a technical nuisance; it is a negotiating sword that the US can unsheathe at any time. A finding of unfair trade practices could trigger unilateral tariffs on Indian goods, potentially undoing whatever the interim pact achieves. The US Supreme Court's recent ruling striking down certain reciprocal tariffs has added legal complexity but has not eliminated the executive branch's authority to act.

## The diaspora stake

For the estimated 4.4 million Indian Americans — and for the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals on work visas — the trade relationship is not an abstraction. It determines whether Indian IT firms can bid for US government contracts, whether Indian pharmaceutical companies can export generics without prohibitive regulatory delays, and whether the H-1B visa programme, which is effectively a subsidy for bilateral services trade, remains politically tenable.

US Ambassador Sergio Gor, speaking at a Confederation of Indian Industry summit this month, framed the relationship in investment terms: Indian firms are building factories, hiring Americans, and contributing to local economies in ways that make the trade deficit a misleading metric. The diplomatic language is designed to insulate the economic relationship from the tariff wars that have dominated headlines.

Whether it works will depend on what happens in June. The delegation's visit will be the first face-to-face negotiation since the Section 301 investigation intensified. Both sides are expected to arrive with opening positions that leave room for compromise — but also with red lines that could, if crossed, send the relationship backward.

The India-US trade deal is closer than it has been in years. It is also more fragile.
